sentences.text: Haestasaurus was a large, four-legged herbivore with a long neck, belonging to the Macronaria group of sauropod dinosaurs.
The only known species within this genus is Haestasaurus becklesii.
A rock block associated with the forelimb, cataloged as NHMUK R1868, holds the distinction of being the first known fossil to preserve parts of sauropod skin.
A 2022 study revealed that the skin scales featured small protuberances and gradually decreased in size, possibly toward the elbow, to allow for greater flexibility.
Collector Samuel Husband Beckles obtained a rock block from the Wealden Sandstone near Hastings, East Sussex, in 1852.
Despite the historical record, the precise location where these fossils were originally found is now unknown.
Paul Upchurch, Philip D. Mannion, and Michael P. Taylor established the separate genus Haestasaurus in 2015 after determining it was distinct from Pelorosaurus conybeari.
The genus name Haestasaurus is derived from the Saxon tribal leader Haesta and the Greek word sauros meaning reptile.
The known forelimb bones include a humerus measuring 599 millimetres, an ulna measuring 421 millimetres, and a radius measuring 404 millimetres.
The preserved area of the skin impression measures 215 mm by 195 mm.
Researchers favor the classification of Haestasaurus as a rare, late-surviving basal member of the Macronaria clade.
The holotype specimen dates to the Berriasian-Valanginian stages of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 140 million years ago.
Haestasaurus lived between 139.1 and 132.6 million years ago during the Berriasian to Valanginian periods.
It is debated whether Haestasaurus belongs to the Titanosauria or is a basal Macronarian, as limited fossil material prevents a single definitive solution.
